01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
ledger
A book used to keep official records.
dispatch
The act of sending something.
layout
The arrangement of a document’s parts.
confirmation
Evidence that something happened.
inventory
A checked list or description of records.
follow up
To check what happened after an earlier action.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's latest update seemed at first to answer the question Emma had asked. The records team had located a ledger headed “Outgoing letters — Student Travel 2011”, apparently maintained by the scheme administrator.

Emma was careful about the word outgoing. A dispatch record might tell her that a notice had been processed for sending; it would not necessarily establish that it had reached the intended applicant.

Fiona described entries containing reference numbers and dates. Other spaces were blank. The team had not compared the ledger with completed notices, and Fiona would not disclose information identifying students. She could not yet offer even a reliable total of entries.

“Could you share its layout rather than its contents?” Emma asked.

Fiona agreed. Later she emailed images of the cover and an unused page. The page carried four headings: reference number, date prepared, date sent and notes. Two separate date columns immediately caught Emma's attention. A prepared notice and a dispatched notice were not automatically the same thing.

Sarah listened while Emma explained.

“Then we can finally prove those students were notified.”

“We can establish that the trust kept a system for recording notices. Fiona says some entries have dates marked as sent. We still have no delivery confirmation.”

“Doesn't a sent date count for something?”

“Of course. But the claim has to match the evidence.”

The newspaper archive also replied. Staff had not yet examined its unpublished correspondence from 2011 and warned that any access might be limited by privacy rules. Emma added the message to her research log without treating the possibility of surviving letters as confirmation of further complaints.

That afternoon Fiona clarified the team's preliminary observations. Several lines in the ledger appeared to contain dispatch dates. No matching postal receipts had been located, and the inventory was not complete. Fiona had not established whether the entries represented every decision, or whether the dates were accurate.

Emma returned to the parent's published complaint. It asked why selection decisions had been unclear, but offered no account of a notice arriving or failing to arrive. She could not connect the anonymous author to a particular ledger entry without more evidence.

She divided a page into three stages: Prepared, Sent, Received. The first two now had documentary headings and some reported entries behind them. The third remained an unverified outcome. Even a correctly completed dispatch register might fail to demonstrate delivery.

Sarah asked what Emma would request next.

“Not names,” Emma said. “The administrator's instructions. Was anyone meant to follow up on letters that weren't received?”

The question was narrower than an allegation that students had been deliberately kept uninformed. It was also something a surviving policy might be able to answer.

For the first time, Emma could see a route from the scheme's written promises towards a test of its actual administration—provided she continued to respect the boundaries of what each document could prove.
